newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Stena Line says 1997 hard to forecast.
newsitem.headline: Stena Line says 1997 hard to forecast.

text.p: Loss-making Swedish ferry operator Stena Line AB said on Tuesday its 1997 performance was very difficult to forecast with a question mark still hanging over its proposed cooperation with Britain's P&O.

"In light of the fact that the authorities have still not taken a position on cooperation with P&O, results' views for the current year are very difficult to predict," Stena Line said in its results statement.
The company posted a loss of 448 million crowns compared to a profit of 201 million crowns. Turnover fell to 9.21 billion crowns from 9.44 billion.
It proposed no dividend compared to a dividend of 0.75 crowns a year earlier.
The result was in line with the company's own expectations for a loss of 450 million crowns.

The two old shipping rivals unveiled plans in October to join forces on three routes across the English Channel, in response to the swift progress made by the tunnel in grabbing a 40 percent market share on the route two years after opening.
In November the British government referred the proposed merger to its main competition watchdog, the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC), for investigation of the deals effects on competition.
It said its key route between Dover, England and Calais, France continued to suffer.
"Operations between England and the continent was signifcantly affected by the pricing and competition situation on Dover-Calais," Stena Line said.
After a fire in Eurotunnel in the autumn, which boosted Stena Line's volumes, it regained its leading market position, Stena Line said. The tunnel also planned more price cuts, Stena Line said.
"The new prices are in the mean time considerably lower than price levels which were proposed before the tunnel prices were halved ahead of the 1996 high season," Stena Line said.
It said outside the Dover-Calais route the group's volumes fell between three and six percent, depending on the traffic category.
Stena Line managing director Bo Lerenius said the planned cooperation would help the group's result in 1998, but not have any effect on Stena's 1997 results.
"There are probably comparable one-off costs we are saving, so it will hit us pretty hard...The signifcant effect will probably be from 1998 and onwards," Lerenius told a news conference.
The joint venture company would save the group at least 780 million crowns of the total fixed costs of 2.9 billion crowns.
"Our expectation is that we will have a decision in the first half of April. This means that the company should be going at the end of April or the beginning of May," he said.
